summary: Defines TLS extensions that let a client and server agree to use OpenPGP certificates for authentication in a TLS session, and describes how to carry those certificates. It also creates a registry for non-X.509 certificate types. It is informational, not standards-track, and obsoletes RFC 5081.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally a secure website shows one kind of ID card. This lets computers show a different kind of ID card, the kind used for secure email.

subtitle: How a TLS client and server agree to authenticate with OpenPGP certificates instead of X.509.

tldr.problem: TLS was defined to use X.509 certificates, so peers that hold OpenPGP certificates had no standard way to use them to authenticate a TLS session.
tldr.mechanism: A cert_type hello extension lets each side list and pick a certificate type, and the Certificate message is changed to carry an OpenPGP certificate, or just its fingerprint, together with the ID of the subkey to use.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 5081 and is not backward-compatible with it. It also sets up the registry for non-X.509 certificate types. It is Informational, not a standard.

today: RFC 6091 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 5081. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why OpenPGP Certificates in TLS
sections.content:
The IETF has two sets of standards for public key certificates: one for X.509 certificates and one for OpenPGP certificates. At the time of writing, RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) defined authentication with X.509 certificates only. RFC 6091 specifies how to negotiate the use of OpenPGP certificates for a TLS session and how to transport them inside TLS.

The extensions are backward-compatible with the existing TLS specification, so implementations that use X.509 are not affected. The document uses the term OpenPGP key as in RFC 4880, and OpenPGP certificate for an OpenPGP key that is enabled for authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS used to accept only one kind of ID card. This note teaches it to accept a second kind too, without bothering anyone who only uses the first.

sections.title: Negotiating the Certificate Type
sections.content:
A client that supports more than one certificate type MUST include an extension of type cert_type in its extended client hello. The extension is assigned the value 9 from the TLS ExtensionType registry. It carries a list of the certificate types the client can use, sorted by client preference, and it MUST be omitted if the client supports only X.509.

The two certificate types are X.509(0) and OpenPGP(1). The same CertificateTypeExtension structure is used by both sides: a client sends a list, while a server sends a single chosen type.

If the server gets a client hello with cert_type and picks a cipher suite that needs a certificate, it MUST either select one of the offered types or end the session with a fatal unsupported_certificate alert. A server that supports only X.509 MAY leave the extension out of its server hello. No new cipher suites are needed: any existing suite whose key exchange suits the key in the certificate can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The client says which ID cards it can show, favourite first. The server picks one it likes, or says it cannot play along.

sections.title: Carrying the Certificate
sections.content:
Once OpenPGP is negotiated, the Certificate message must hold an OpenPGP certificate in binary OpenPGP format, containing everything required by Section 11.1 of RFC 4880. Its public key has to fit the key exchange: an RSA key usable for encryption for RSA, a DSA key usable for authentication for DHE_DSS, and an RSA key usable for authentication for DHE_RSA.

Each certificate is tagged with a descriptor type. With subkey_cert, the certificate is sent in full along with an OpenPGPKeyID naming the subkey to use, which must be given even when the certificate has only a primary key. With subkey_cert_fingerprint, only the primary key fingerprint and the subkey ID are sent. If the peer cannot find a certificate with that fingerprint, it answers with a fatal certificate_unobtainable alert, defined in RFC 6066. It is RECOMMENDED that keys used with this protocol have the authentication flag (0x20) set.

The other handshake messages mostly follow TLS. In a Certificate Request, the certificate_authorities list MUST be empty when OpenPGP is negotiated. A client with no certificate MUST send an empty_cert structure, and the server SHOULD answer with a fatal handshake_failure alert if client authentication is required.
sections.plainLanguage: The ID card can be handed over whole, or you can just give its serial number and let the other side look it up. You also say which of the keys on the card to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations of RFC 5246, RFC 6066 and RFC 4880 apply. Trust questions such as the web of trust and how certificates are verified are outside the scope and are left to the application layer protocols.

The document argues that certificate type negotiation works like cipher suite negotiation, so its security properties are believed to be the same. When fingerprints are sent instead of full certificates, the discussion of Client Certificate URLs in RFC 6066 applies, especially if external servers are used to fetch keys. Unlike that extension, here an unsent certificate is always identified by its fingerprint, which serves as a cryptographic hash of the certificate. Eavesdroppers can learn the number and types of certificates the parties hold, plus the certificate contents, when confidentiality is not available from a previous handshake.
sections.plainLanguage: Who you decide to trust is up to the programs on top. This note only says how to show the card, and it is no easier to trick than picking a cipher.

sections.title: The Certificate Types Registry
sections.content: The document reuses the cert_type extension and the registry originally defined in RFC 5081, and the existing IANA references now point to RFC 6091. In the "TLS Certificate Types" registry, values 0 (X.509) and 1 (OpenPGP) are defined here. Values 2 through 223 are assigned by "RFC Required", and values 224 through 255 are reserved for Private Use.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a numbered list of ID card types. Two numbers are taken, some are held for future types, and some are left free for private use.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 5081
sections.content:
RFC 5081 required that an OpenPGP key or subkey carry the authentication flag, so authentication failed if the flag was missing or was set on more than one subkey. RFC 6091 instead marks the subkey ID explicitly in the Server Certificate and Client Certificate messages, which places no limit on the contents of the OpenPGP certificates that can be used.

This change makes implementations of the two documents incompatible. The authors reuse the OpenPGP CertificateType value with different semantics and believe this causes no interoperability issues because RFC 5081 was not widely deployed. The old cert and cert_fingerprint descriptor types are marked obsolete: empty_cert replaces cert, and cert_fingerprint MUST NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The old version only worked if exactly one key on the card had a special sticker. The new version just says which key to use, so any card works.

messages.label: ClientHello + cert_type
messages.note: Lists supported certificate types in order of preference.

messages.label: ServerHello + cert_type
messages.note: Names the single type chosen, or the server ends the session with unsupported_certificate.

items.label: empty_cert
items.desc: An empty certificate, used when a client has none to offer.

items.label: subkey_cert
items.desc: The full certificate plus the ID of the subkey to use.

items.label: subkey_cert_fingerprint
items.desc: Primary key fingerprint plus the subkey ID, instead of the certificate.
